Security and privacy

What Seamless protects and from whom - what a fresh install does, what can leave your computer, the five layers you can add, and the limits, stated plainly.

Seamless holds what your agents learn about your work: its rules, its decisions, sometimes the names of its clients. This page is the map of how that is protected. It covers what a fresh install does, what can leave your computer, the five layers you can add when the work calls for them, and what none of them cover. Each layer has a guide of its own; this page says what each one is for and links there.

What Seamless defends against

An agent is capable and usually well behaved, and it can still be tricked. A web page, an issue, an email or a file it reads can carry instructions, and an agent that follows them acts with everything it can reach. Seamless is built around that case. Each layer narrows what a tricked agent can read, what it can plant for the sessions that come after it, and what it can open without you.

The other risks are the usual ones for software that runs on your computer: a program elsewhere on your network, another account on the same computer, a release that is not what it claims to be, and lost data.

A fresh install

A Standalone install, the installer's default, starts like this:

  • It answers this computer only. The daemon listens on 127.0.0.1:8081, and a request naming any host it does not serve gets 421, which closes DNS rebinding.
  • A key guards it. The first run writes a random 32-byte key into ~/.config/seamless/seamless.yaml with 0600 permissions. The agent registrations read it from there when they connect; none copies it into the agent's own config (how). The console signs in with it, or with a passkey once you switch to passkey sign-in.
  • Your knowledge is files on your disk. Memories and notes are markdown under ~/.seamless, and sessions, tasks and events live in a SQLite file beside them. There is no Seamless account and no hosted service.
  • It backs itself up. A release install takes a backup every day and keeps the last seven, in ~/.seamless/backups. A restore can be undone (backups).
  • Updates prove where they came from before they install (below).

Every project starts open, and the five layers below start off.

What leaves your computer

Seamless sends no usage data. On its own it makes one kind of request: a release build asks GitHub's release list for new versions every six hours, anonymously, and an install the installer made downloads the updates it installs. update.check: false turns all of that off.

Everything else is something you set up or an agent asked for:

  • A model provider, once you add its key. With OpenAI or Anthropic configured, the text of every memory and note is sent to the provider to be embedded, from every project, fenced and locked ones included, and so is each recall query. The gardener's monthly digests send a project's session findings to the chat model, and gardener_request and gardener_split call it when an agent invokes them. Ollama keeps all of it on your computer. With no provider, recall runs on full-text search alone.
  • capture_url fetches only the URLs an agent asks for, on ports 80 and 443, and refuses private, loopback and link-local addresses.
  • Your own computers. A networked Client talks to your Server.
  • The Touch ID approver, if you choose to download it.

Two things are outside Seamless's reach: what it puts in an agent's context travels to that agent's model provider with the rest of the conversation, and the agent's own client keeps its transcripts.

The five layers

The console's Privacy screen draws these for your own server: which are on, which wait on an earlier one, and how far a compromised agent gets in each arrangement.

1. Project fences

A project is open by default and shares the way a personal knowledge base should. Make it confidential and nothing in it reaches an agent working in another project, whether through briefings, recall, tool reads, family surfaces or the gardener. Make it sealed and nothing outside reaches in either: global memories and family stop at its edge. A refusal never echoes the content it protects.

With access requests on, an agent that needs a fenced project asks, and you approve a read-only or read-and-write grant, or a move of the whole conversation into the project. What a conversation writes after reading fenced content carries a provenance stamp (project isolation).

A fence binds what Seamless serves. Until layer 3 it does not stop an agent that reads ~/.seamless directly, and it trusts the session an agent says it belongs to.

2. Write screening

Briefings and recall make the shared memory the most leveraged place to plant a prompt injection: a poisoned constraint reaches every session until someone notices. Write screening checks every agent write to a memory or note, on your computer, for secrets, instructions aimed at agents, hidden text and characters, long encoded blobs and links outside an allowlist.

  • A write that fails waits on the console's Held screen until you release or discard it, and the agent is told not to rephrase its way past the hold.
  • A supersede or delete of a constraint is always held, and so is a change to a rule from a session that read outside text.
  • Injected memories say whether you confirmed them or an agent wrote them.
  • A memory or note file changed on disk by anything but Seamless is quarantined until you accept it, and a lockdown switch narrows briefings to what you confirmed.

It is off by default, and the console's Home welcome card offers it after install (write screening). The screens are heuristics: they catch the known shapes of an attack and surface the rest for review.

3. Seamless in its own account

Out of the box Seamless runs as you, so any program of yours can read its files and its key. peer_auth moves it into an operating-system account of its own with a 0700 data directory, and serves agents on a Unix socket where the kernel reports each caller's account. Your agents reach Seamless through that socket, and its data directory is out of their reach. The daemon refuses to start if another account could rewrite its data, its socket's directory, its config or its binary (peer_auth).

4. Locked projects

Under peer_auth you can lock a project. A locked project is closed to every agent, its own included, until you approve one:

  • in a terminal of your own, with seam approve and your password;
  • in the console, with a passkey;
  • with Touch ID, through the optional Seamless Approve app on a Mac with Apple silicon.

An approval is a lease on that agent's process tree, as the kernel reports it, for the session, an hour or four hours, capped at eight hours unless you change the cap. The Touch ID prompt is built from the daemon's facts, never from the agent's own words, so a request cannot dress itself up as something else (locked projects).

5. Restricted agent accounts

Run unattended agents as an operating-system account of their own and list it under peer_auth.restricted. That account reaches the open, unlocked projects, or only the ones you name. It reads global memories without writing them, cannot create projects or ask for access, and its changes to binding rules wait for you on the Held screen (restricted local accounts).

Your other computers

Networked mode shares one daemon across your computers with no service in between (networked Seamless):

  • The Server gets a name and a certificate at setup and serves https, TLS 1.2 or later.
  • A Client checks the Server's certificate fingerprint, then pairs with a one-time code: 80 bits, ten minutes, used once, stored hashed. Pairing over plain http is refused.
  • On macOS and Linux the Client runs a relay that pins the Server's exact certificate, holds a client certificate of its own, and reports each local caller's account and process chain. A Windows Client holds a key of its own and never opens a locked project.
  • Every paired device can be revoked on the console's Devices page.

Your own network or tailnet is the boundary. The public internet is not a supported one.

Releases and updates

  • The installers check every archive against the release's checksums.txt, and that file against the maintainer's hardware-key signature (checksums.txt.sshsig, on every release after v0.8.3) using the keys they carry. With cosign installed they also verify its Sigstore signature.
  • seamlessd update, and every automatic update, verifies the release's installer and checksums.txt against their Sigstore bundles in-process, pinned to this repository's release workflow at that exact tag and to a trusted root built into the binary, before it runs anything.
  • macOS binaries are signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple.
  • An automatic update waits a day after a release is published, backs up first, and rolls back if the new version does not come up.
  • update.release_signers pins the maintainer's keys, so that every later update needs their signature as well (owner-signed releases).

A fresh install trusts the site that serves the installer. Read the script first if that boundary matters to you.

For a security monitor

Two optional outputs let a separate tool watch what agents do without reading what they wrote: a metadata feed of every event to a Unix socket you name, and a commit-matching snapshot of the sessions and tasks that recorded each commit (security monitor). Both are off by default.

What Seamless does not claim

  • No encryption at rest. Memories and notes are plain markdown, the database is plain SQLite, and backups are not encrypted. Disk encryption is the operating system's job.
  • Your own account, without layer 3. Any program running as you can read ~/.seamless and the key, whatever the fences say.
  • Root. Root, and anyone who can become the daemon's account, reads everything. A passwordless sudo to it voids the arrangement.
  • What a session already read. An approval that ends does not unread what is in the agent's transcript.
  • Seamless guards its own surfaces. An agent can still copy what it read into a file, a commit or a pull request.
  • Hooks fail open. A daemon that is down never blocks an agent, so a session can start without its briefing.
  • Your model provider. Text you send for embeddings goes to the provider you configure (above).
  • Windows has no peer_auth, relay or Server role.

Choosing a setup

You want Turn on Guide
One person, one computer, ordinary projects Nothing: a Standalone install Quickstart
Client work that must not leak into other projects confidential or sealed on those projects Project isolation
Agents that read the web, issues or email Write screening Write screening
A project even your own agents open only with your approval peer_auth, then lock the project peer_auth
Unattended agents with a narrower reach A restricted agent account Restricted accounts
One memory across your computers Networked mode Network install

Report a security problem

Report a vulnerability privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, not in a public issue. The repository's security policy says what is in scope.
